rules.title: Account is in a root-equivalent group
rules.subject: {name}
rules.why: Members of docker, lxd, incus and libvirt control a hypervisor or container engine that runs as root and can mount the host's disks; members of disk can read and write raw disks directly. Each is root by another name.
rules.fix: Remove the membership unless the account is meant to be an administrator (gpasswd -d <user> <group>), and treat remaining members as root.

rules.title: Account can read password hashes
rules.subject: {name}
rules.why: The shadow group can read /etc/shadow, so a member can try to crack every account's password offline, root's included.
rules.fix: Remove the membership (gpasswd -d <user> shadow). Only programs, not people, should be in this group.

rules.title: Account can read system logs
rules.subject: {name}
rules.why: The adm group can read most of /var/log. Logs regularly capture secrets: passwords typed into the wrong prompt, tokens in URLs, command lines.
rules.fix: Remove the membership unless the account reviews logs for a living.

rules.title: Passwordless sudo for any command
rules.subject: {who} ({source}): {raw}
rules.why: Anything that runs as this account, a compromised browser tab's download or a malicious package's install script included, becomes root without a password prompt.
rules.fix: Remove NOPASSWD so sudo asks for the password, or limit the rule to the specific commands that need it.

rules.title: Passwordless sudo for a program that can run commands or write files
rules.subject: {who} ({source}): {command}
rules.why: This program can start a shell, run other commands or write any file, so being allowed to run it as root without a password is the same as passwordless root.
rules.fix: Remove the rule, require the password, or replace it with a narrow wrapper script owned by root that does only the one job needed.

rules.title: sudo rule runs a program that can be overwritten
rules.subject: {who} ({source}): {command_path}
rules.why: sudo runs this program as root. Whoever can overwrite it decides what runs the next time someone uses the rule.
rules.fix: Make the program owned by root and writable only by root, or point the rule at a copy in a root-owned folder.

rules.title: sudo rule uses a wildcard
rules.subject: {who} ({source}): {command}
rules.why: Wildcards in sudo rules match far more than they appear to: extra arguments, other files, path tricks. They are a common way a narrow rule turns into a broad one.
rules.fix: List the exact commands and arguments instead of using '*', or use sudoedit for editing files.

rules.title: sudo keeps the caller's environment or library paths
rules.subject: {source}: {setting}
rules.why: If sudo passes library or interpreter search paths through, the caller can make any command they may run with sudo load their own code as root.
rules.fix: Keep env_reset on and remove these variables from env_keep.

rules.title: Another account's SSH private key is readable
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Whoever can read the key can log in wherever it is accepted, as its owner, unless it has a passphrase.
rules.fix: chmod 600 the key and 700 the .ssh folder. If others could read it, replace the key and remove the old public key from authorized_keys everywhere.

rules.title: Another account's credential file or history is readable
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: These files hold passwords and tokens in plain text, and shell history often catches secrets typed on the command line.
rules.fix: chmod 600 the file (700 its folder) and rotate any credential it holds.

rules.title: Shell history file present
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Shell history keeps every command typed, including passwords and tokens passed on the command line.
rules.fix: Review it and clear anything sensitive. Keep secrets off the command line (read them from a file or a prompt instead).
